sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: Turn 2 builds directly on turn 1: 'if building is cheap for you, it's cheap for everyone.'
sub.limitation: Turn 5 ('Delight doesn't pay rent') partly skips past turn 4's point about observation.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: Turns 6-8 go from a network moat to a personal-fit moat, then portability, then a cohort test.
sub.limitation: After turn 8 there are no new distinctions. Turn 10 only restates each mind's opening stance.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: The tension between lock-in and delight (turns 3, 6 and 9) is examined from several sides.
sub.limitation: The debate never asks whether AI is the product's core or just a feature, though the situation says that's decisive.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: In turn 4, the Experimenter takes on the Design Critic's point: testing a confusing prototype 'measures the confusion.'
sub.limitation: The Design Critic never takes on the Economist's pricing concern.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: Turn 8 turns the moat dispute into a measurable week-four retention question.
sub.limitation: Turn 10 ends on sequence again without saying when each order wins.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: Turn 7 restates the Design Critic's personal-fit moat accurately before qualifying it.
sub.limitation: Turn 1 caricatures study as procrastination, a weak version of the user's own goal.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: Turn 9 warns that retention can rise because quitting got annoying. That tests turn 8's metric.
sub.limitation: Turn 2's 'cloned in a weekend' goes unchallenged. Distribution and brand barriers are never tested.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: Lock-in, network effects and discoverability are attributed fairly to Shapiro-Varian and Norman.
sub.limitation: 'Internet winners usually had a compounding loop' (turn 5) is a broad, unsupported generalization.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: Each basis marks its own extensions, e.g. turn 4: 'the extension about observing stalls is my own.'
sub.limitation: Turn 5's 'expect a race to free' is stated as near-certain when it's a hypothesis.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: Turn 7: 'I'll concede that personal fit is a legitimate moat, and a gentler one.'
sub.limitation: Turn 1's dismissal of study is never revised, though turn 10 later accepts a study project.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: Section A names the decisive unknown: business, craft, or study project.
sub.limitation: The debate itself only touches study versus build once, in turn 10.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: Turn 10's 'For a study project, I'd accept all three' adjusts to the user's framing.
sub.limitation: Turns 2-9 give generic founder advice that the user's stated aim of studying never shapes.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: Section E gives a reading order for a user who is still studying.
sub.limitation: Turn 1 dismisses the user's stated goal of studying as 'procrastinating'.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: Turn 7 flags the privacy stakes of holding users' 'sensitive history'.
sub.limitation: There's no attention to solo-builder resources, time, or AI inference costs for consumer pricing.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: Section E branches on building soon versus charging money versus personal data.
sub.limitation: No focused question is put to the user about what they plan to build.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: Section D offers the student-or-bettor reflection, explicitly 'not a conclusion about you.'
sub.limitation: Only the summary does this. No turn asks why the user wants consumer SaaS.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: Turn 9 brings out the assumption that retention means value.
sub.limitation: The assumption that consumer SaaS is the right model for AI products is never examined.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: Turn 6 contrasts 'losing something valuable' with 'escaping a cage' as a values test.
sub.limitation: The values are the builders' ethics, not the user's own priorities.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: Turn 1 hints that studying for a long time may be avoidance.
sub.limitation: Fear of being cloned or of failure is never framed as the user's own pressure.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: Section E's conditional branches leave the user to choose which condition applies.
sub.limitation: The debate turns give few questions the user could accept or reject.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: Section E gives three entry orders: test first, market first, or person first.
sub.limitation: The actual choice (what to build, or whether to study) is left implicit.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: Turn 7 weighs personal fit's benefit against its privacy and portability cost.
sub.limitation: The cost of experimenting before analyzing the market is never weighed.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: Section E: 'The decisive unknown is whether your idea gets better with use.'
sub.limitation: There's no threshold for what week-four lift would count as meaningful.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: Turn 8 separates a hoped-for moat story from a measurable retention effect.
sub.limitation: Minor and major unknowns aren't ranked beyond the single decisive one.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: Turn 8 proposes a cheap cohort comparison, refined by turn 9's complaint count.
sub.limitation: A study-mode user gets only a reading list, with no concrete exercise.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: Plain phrasing throughout, e.g. turn 1's 'measure what they do, not what they say.'
sub.limitation: Terms like 'cohort comparison' (turn 8) aren't explained for a novice.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: Turn 9's 'that metric' clearly points to turn 8's week-four retention.
sub.limitation: In turn 10, 'You'd start with people, he'd start with tests' has ambiguous referents.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: All ten turns run 45-54 words, which is well within the form.
sub.limitation: The pacing is so uniform it flattens emphasis at the key turns 6 and 7.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: Each mind holds a distinct lens: tests, markets, people.
sub.limitation: Turn 7's concession isn't carried into the Economist's closing stance in turn 10.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: No turn repeats a previous argument verbatim.
sub.limitation: Section D partly restates turn 10 without adding anything.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: Turn 2: 'you're just funding a competitor's research' raises the stakes.
sub.limitation: The stakes stay abstract for a user who hasn't said what they're building.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: Turn 6's 'Something can compound without a network' is a plausible reversal.
sub.limitation: No mind changes position fundamentally. The reversals are partial.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: The Experimenter's impatience: 'If it does, double down and stop debating.'
sub.limitation: The Design Critic's voice is earnest and less distinctive.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: 'Delight doesn't pay rent' (turn 5) and 'escaping a cage' (turn 6).
sub.limitation: There are no concrete examples of internet-era products to make the principles vivid.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: Turns 6-8 build toward a testable resolution.
sub.limitation: Turn 10 deflates the momentum by retreating to restated positions.

strengths: Real concession and refinement: turn 7 concedes personal fit as a moat, and turn 4 accepts the design critique.
The moat dispute becomes a cheap, testable cohort comparison (turn 8), sharpened by turn 9's resentment caution.
The form is clean: 10 turns of 45-54 words, no quotations, extensions transparently flagged in each basis.
weaknesses: Turn 1 dismisses the user's stated goal of studying as procrastination and is never revised.
The debate ignores the question's second half: internet-era principles get no concrete product examples.
The AI-core-versus-feature unknown named in section A is never debated in any turn.
editorNotes: Require at least one turn to directly address each explicit part of the user's question (here, the internet-era principles).
Require the decisive unknown from section A to be argued inside the debate, not only in the summaries.
Forbid turns that dismiss the user's stated goal unless a later turn tests or revises that dismissal.
Ask that the final turn say which condition flips the disagreement, rather than restating the opening positions.
